passage: The 6:10 local was packed, and Manjula had only until Dadar to say it. Wedged by the door, she leaned toward Devika. "You hardly spoke in the client call today. When they asked about the delay, you knew the answer, I saw you mouth it. And last week in the budget review, you let Arvind present your numbers." The train screeched. Devika's face went hot. She wanted to say that Arvind always talks over everyone, that the clients never asked her directly. The words were ready on her tongue. Instead she held the rail and said, "Give me one more example." Manjula did. At Dadar, Manjula squeezed her arm and stepped off. Devika stayed standing, replaying the call, the sting still there but duller.

qa.q: Until which station did Manjula have to say it?
qa.a: Manjula had only until Dadar to say it.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling when the words of defence were ready on her tongue?
qa.a: She felt stung and embarrassed, and part of her wanted to protect herself by blaming Arvind and the clients.

qa.q: What did Devika's choice to ask for one more example do for her?
qa.a: It turned the sting into information; instead of defending, she took in more of what was useful, which gives her something concrete to change.

qa.q: What might it have cost Manjula to give this feedback on a crowded train?
qa.a: She may have worried about hurting Devika in a rushed, public place, yet chose honesty because the pattern was already showing in client calls.

grounding: On a crowded commute a mentor tells a young woman, with examples, that she stays silent in meetings; it stings and she chooses to absorb rather than defend.

passage: Binita had expected Tenzin to talk about her pitch deck. Instead, in the corner booth of the Hyderabad office cafeteria, he opened his notebook. "Three things from this week. Monday's stand-up, you nodded while Ravi claimed the vendor idea, and it was yours. Wednesday, you messaged me your view after the meeting instead of saying it in the meeting. Thursday, you said 'sorry, small point' before the best point in the room." He closed the notebook. "People are starting to think you have nothing to say." Binita's jaw tightened. "I'm just not loud like Ravi." "You don't need to be loud." She stirred her coffee for a long moment. "Okay," she said finally. "Which one hurt me most?"

qa.q: What did Binita say before the best point in the room on Thursday?
qa.a: She said 'sorry, small point' before the best point in the room.

qa.q: What does Binita's tight jaw and "I'm just not loud like Ravi" suggest?
qa.a: She feels stung and a bit defensive, trying to explain the feedback away before letting it in.

qa.q: What shows Binita beginning to absorb the feedback rather than defend it?
qa.a: After stirring her coffee, she asks which example hurt her most, turning the sting into a question she can act on.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel while Binita stirs her coffee in silence?
qa.a: He is probably a little tense, unsure whether she will shut down, and relieved when she comes back with a real question.

grounding: A mentor gives a young woman three concrete examples of staying quiet in meetings; she bristles, then decides to take in what is useful.

passage:
Subject: Thank you (and a little defensiveness)
Hi Mahima,
I've been thinking about what you said on Friday: that I speak too little in the Monday meetings. You gave me three examples, the vendor issue, the delay I spotted, and the budget question I asked you afterwards instead of in the room.
Honestly, my first reaction was to defend myself. I wanted to say I'm careful, not quiet. My father always told me, "Beti, speak only when you're sure." I think I took that a bit too far.
But all three examples were right. So this week I'll try one thing: say one point in the meeting, even if I'm only eighty per cent sure.
Could we check in after Monday?
Aditi

qa.q: How many examples did Mahima give?
qa.a: Three examples.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling on first hearing the feedback?
qa.a: Aditi felt stung and defensive, wanting to reply that being careful is not the same as being quiet.

qa.q: What choice does Aditi make at this stage, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Aditi absorbs the useful part and tries one small step, saying one point in the meeting, instead of only arguing back.

qa.q: How might Mahima feel reading this email?
qa.a: Mahima is likely relieved and glad that the direct feedback was taken as help rather than an attack.

grounding: Shows a mentee stung by a mentor's feedback about speaking too little in meetings, choosing to absorb what is useful.

passage:
You want to know the hardest thing anyone said to me at work, as the only woman on the design team? Thomas, my mentor. We were having chai and he said, "Farida, you disappear in meetings." Just like that.
I laughed, then I didn't. He gave me examples. The client call where I had the answer and let my manager say it. The design review where I nodded at a mistake. It stung so much that I nearly told him he didn't understand how loud that room is.
But I went home and wrote down every meeting from that month. He was right about most of them. Not all. So next week, in the review, I made myself speak first. My hands were shaking. Nobody noticed, except Thomas, who gave me a small nod.

qa.q: What did Thomas say to Farida over chai?
qa.a: "Farida, you disappear in meetings."

qa.q: How did Farida feel when Thomas gave her examples?
qa.a: She felt stung and defensive, almost telling him he didn't understand how loud the room was.

qa.q: What did Farida do that helped her decide what was useful?
qa.a: She wrote down every meeting from that month and checked the feedback, finding it right about most but not all.

qa.q: What might Thomas have felt when he gave Farida the small nod?
qa.a: He was likely pleased and proud that she took the hard feedback and spoke first.

grounding: Shows a mentee stung by feedback that she speaks too little in meetings, testing it, and absorbing what is useful.

passage:
Monday: Anirban caught Minakshi after the team meeting. "You had the best idea about the survey and didn't say it. That's the third time this month." She went red and said she'd been about to.
Wednesday: Minakshi still felt the sting. She drafted a long message explaining why the room was too fast for her, then deleted it. Instead she wrote three points on a sticky note for Friday.
Friday: Halfway through the meeting, Minakshi read out her first point. Her voice wobbled, but two people wrote it down. Anirban didn't say anything. He just caught her eye and nodded.

qa.q: What did Minakshi write on the sticky note?
qa.a: Three points for Friday.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling on Wednesday when she drafted and deleted the long message?
qa.a: She still felt stung and defensive, but chose not to send an excuse and to try something instead.

qa.q: What turning point did Minakshi reach between Monday and Friday?
qa.a: She moved from defending herself to absorbing the feedback and planning three points to say in the meeting.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel when Minakshi reads out her point?
qa.a: He is probably pleased and relieved that his direct feedback helped rather than hurt the relationship.

grounding: Shows a mentee stung by feedback that she speaks too little in meetings, over several days choosing to absorb it.

passage: Bhavna, sit, and I'll tell you what my old boss Mrs Pinto told me when I was twenty-five. I, Gargi, was the quiet one on the team, and proud of it. I thought I was being thoughtful. One evening she called me in and said, "You speak too little in meetings." Then she gave examples. "On Monday you had the right numbers and let Suresh present the wrong ones. On Thursday the client asked about delays and you looked at your notebook." My ears went hot. I wanted to say, "I'm just not a show-off." I had the sentence ready. Instead I went home, sat on the balcony and made two lists: what she said that was unfair, and what was true. The second list was longer. That is the choice, Bhavna: defend yourself, or take what is useful.

qa.q: What did Gargi do when the client asked about delays?
qa.a: Gargi looked at the notebook.

qa.q: What was the young Gargi feeling when her ears went hot?
qa.a: She felt stung and defensive, with a ready answer that she was just not a show-off.

qa.q: What choice did Gargi make on the balcony, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Instead of defending herself, she listed what was unfair and what was true, and found the true list longer, which let her use the feedback.

qa.q: What might Mrs Pinto have been hoping for when she gave examples?
qa.a: She probably believed in Gargi and hoped that specific examples would make the feedback useful rather than simply hurtful.

grounding: Shows a mentor giving direct, specific feedback about speaking too little in meetings, and the mentee choosing to absorb what is useful rather than defend.
